surface: wanderwiki: the microsite /apps/wanderwiki/ (Persuade), plus /apps/wanderwiki/privacy/, /apps/wanderwiki/support/ and the two alternatives pages that target it, /alternatives/wikipedia-app/ and /alternatives/kiwix/ (Read variants of the same world)

dossier.mechanism: WanderWiki turns Wikipedia into a finite deck of one-article cards on iPhone. It has three modes: Random draws from the whole encyclopedia. For You draws from 10 interests you declare, each mapped to the chosen edition's own category tree (German + Science queries Wissenschaft, Physik, Chemie, not 'Science' translated). Today in History comes from Wikipedia's official On This Day feed (Selected, Events, Births, Deaths, Holidays). It covers 33 language editions, each read as its own encyclopedia. A card's best outcome is that you stop swiping and read the article: a calm reading view with inline CC BY-SA attribution, saved offline into folders, or surfaced again tomorrow by a widget. There are no ads, no behavioural tracking and no account.
dossier.audienceScene: Mostly on a phone, arriving from Google or an AI answer after typing 'swipe Wikipedia app', 'random Wikipedia articles app', 'Today in History app', 'WikiCards alternative' or 'Wikipedia app alternative'. Three real people. (1) The curious generalist who misses desktop 'Random article' and wants something for the five-minute windows that used to be feed time: the kettle, the coffee queue, between meetings. (2) The multilingual reader of German, Finnish or Japanese Wikipedia who finds every other swiper English-only. (3) The feed-quitter rebuilding a calm, finite reading habit. Desktop visitors from AI answers need the QR to get the app onto their iPhone. Most read in daylight in short windows; the maker's own ritual is the morning.
dossier.culturalHome: Wikipedia's own rituals: 'Random article', the Main Page's 'On this day' box, the languages sidebar, the CC BY-SA licence line. Before the web: the tear-off day calendar with reading on the back of each leaf, the almanac, the page-a-day block, the library card catalogue and Otlet's Mundaneum, teletext pages, shortwave dials naming the world's stations, airmail letters and stamps from abroad, and dual-language editions. And the anti-feed culture of 2024–26: deleting social apps, calm technology, reading instead of scrolling (the journal's 'reading without a feed').
dossier.mustProve: Three things in one screen. (1) The offer: Wikipedia as a swipe deck on iPhone, in 33 language editions, with three modes, no ads and no account. (2) One thing no rival can show: the native category mapping (German + Science gives Wissenschaft, Physik, Chemie, not 'Science' translated), or the 33 editions present in their own scripts. (3) The action and the price: the official badge (plus the QR on desktop), 'Free 3-day trial, then $1.99/mo, $8.99/yr or $24.99 lifetime', and 'iPhone, iOS 18.2+'.
dossier.categoryDefault: The 'knowledge app' page: a deep navy starfield with a glowing globe, gold sparkles and an open book ('Unlock a universe of knowledge'), two iPhone mockups of fanned swipe cards on the right, 'the TikTok of Wikipedia', a badge row, then three equal feature cards (Random / For You / Today) and an FAQ. The app's own icon (puzzle globe, orbit swoosh, gold stars, open book) already sits in this rut, and the app UI's black full-bleed cards pull towards it.
dossier.predictableOpposite: A white Wikipedia look-alike: a Linux-Libertine-style serif wordmark, link-blue text, grey hairlines, an infobox and a hatnote, i.e. 'just Wikipedia'. It is calm, but it impersonates the Wikimedia Foundation (WanderWiki is explicitly not affiliated) and could sell any reader app.
dossier.literalReading: 'Wander' read literally means trail maps, compasses, hiking signposts and footprints between articles; 'card deck' read literally means playing cards. Only candidate 6 (the orienteering map) uses the wander reading, and the Swiss trail-blade version of it already belongs to EarnLock.

candidates.name: The tear-off day calendar with reading on the back of every leaf (Abreißkalender, отрывной календарь, Page-A-Day)
candidates.why: This was the pre-web 'random article': Soviet and German tear-off blocks printed a short piece of reading, an anniversary or a recipe on the back of each day, and page-a-day 'on this day' blocks still sell. It carries Today in History natively (a date on the front, the five categories as its entries), one leaf at a time as the deck, tearing as the swipe, and a block that visibly runs out, so the session is finite rather than a feed. It is the most familiar of the seven.

candidates.name: The card catalogue as Otlet's Mundaneum
candidates.why: Paul Otlet's Répertoire bibliographique universel (Brussels and Mons, from 1895) filed the world's knowledge on 12.5 × 7.5 cm cards in oak drawers, under a decimal classification whose numbers read the same in every language. It is the 'paper Wikipedia' Wikipedians already love. It carries For You as the drawers of your declared interests, Random as pulling any card, folders as your own drawer, and the language-neutral notation as the per-language category mapping. Its risk is oak-and-cream bookishness.

candidates.name: Teletext (Yle Teksti-TV, BBC Ceefax)
candidates.why: Europe's free, ad-light public information service before the web, still on air in Finland. Numbered pages, subpages that rotate 1/4…4/4 (a finite deck) and the Fastext colour keys carry the modes as page numbers. The G0 national character sets, which swap glyphs per language, carry the 33-editions idea down to the alphabet. The studio's own style C ('Page 100') is this exact world.

candidates.name: The world-band receiver dial (Weltempfänger)
candidates.why: A multi-band dial glass printed with stations and cities. Each station broadcasts its own programme in its own language rather than a dub, just as each Wikipedia edition writes its own articles. It carries edition choice as tuning, Random as the scan button, Today in History as the time signal and the finite session as switching off.

candidates.name: Airmail under the Universal Postal Union: the air letter, PAR AVION labels, stamp sheets
candidates.why: The pale-blue aerogramme that folds into its own envelope, labels printed in French plus the national language, red-and-blue chevrons, perforated stamp sheets, and the rule that an address is written the way the destination reads it. It carries the 33 editions as a sheet of stamps and the native category mapping as native addressing (German Science goes to Wissenschaft, Physik, Chemie). 'No enclosures' stands for no ads, and getting the app onto your iPhone becomes delivery.

candidates.name: The orienteering map with IOF pictorial control descriptions
candidates.why: Finland's forest sport (Jukola): a purple course runs from a start triangle through numbered control circles to a finish double circle, with control descriptions drawn as language-independent pictograms. It carries a session as a short course of two or three controls that really ends at a finish, and the pictogram sheet as navigation in any language. It uses the name's literal 'wander', and the Swiss trail-blade version already belongs to EarnLock.

candidates.name: The polyglot / facing-page dual-language edition (Loeb, Complutensian Polyglot)
candidates.why: The book built for reading two languages at once: Loeb's facing pages (green cloth for Greek, red for Latin) and the Complutensian Polyglot's parallel columns, each script in its own fount. It carries the journal's own thesis, that editions are written rather than translated, by pairing an edition's original words (Wissenschaft, Physik, Chemie; the On This Day keys; the endonyms) with WanderWiki's English reading. It makes the 33 scripts the page's only ornament.

styles.label: Par Avion
styles.lineage: International airmail stationery under the Universal Postal Union, whose working language is French. The air letter or aerogramme: one prepaid pale-blue sheet that folds into its own envelope, with printed dashed fold lines, 'Fold here · Plier ici' and 'No enclosures' warnings. Also the blue PAR AVION label with its English or national-language line, red-and-blue chevron borders, perforated stamp sheets with marginal inscriptions, the round date cancel, and the convention that an address is written the way the destination reads it, with only the country line in a lingua franca. Grammar only: no postal operator's name, post horn, crown or real stamp design.
styles.thesis: The page is one air letter unfolded. Wikipedia arrives from 33 editions, each addressed the way its own edition reads (German + Science goes to Wissenschaft, Physik, Chemie, not to 'Science' translated). The editions are a sheet of stamps, 'no enclosures' is the no-ads rule, and the App Store badge delivers the app to your iPhone. It refuses the starry-globe 'universe of knowledge' page with fanned phone mockups, and the white Wikipedia look-alike.
styles.scene: A reader at a kitchen table by a north-facing window in soft morning daylight, opening the day's post over coffee → light.
styles.colorStrategy: Committed. Aerogramme blue is the ground of every surface. Airmail blue and red carry the sheet edge, the labels and the primary action. Cancel violet is used only for dates and cancels. Label white is reserved for stamps, the address label, forms and the badge mount.

type.display: Bricolage Grotesque, variable (@fontsource-variable/bricolage-grotesque, the opsz + wght file, latin 77 KB). The H1 is set at opsz 96 / 800: 112px on desktop, 48px on mobile. Panel titles use opsz 72 / 700 at 44–56px. PAR AVION labels and the stamp codes (de, fi, ja) are caps at opsz 24 / 800, tracked +0.06em. Prices and dates use tabular figures.
type.text: Ysabeau Office 400 and 600 (@fontsource/ysabeau-office, latin 31 KB for both). The letter body is 19px/1.6 on desktop and 17px on mobile; label small print is 14px 600. The cyrillic (9 KB), greek (6 KB), latin-ext (15 KB) and vietnamese (6 KB) slices load through unicode-range only where an endonym needs them.
type.utility: None; no monospace. Hebrew, Arabic, Devanagari, Thai, Han, kana and Hangul endonyms use the visitor's system faces.
type.rationale: Bricolage Grotesque comes from the French grotesque line of Antique Olive, and the UPU prints its labels in French. Its optical-size axis gives the tight, characterful cut for 'Par avion' and the H1 and calm small sizes for stamp codes, from one file. Ysabeau Office is a humanist sans built on Garamond bones with real Cyrillic, Greek and Vietnamese (checked: Č ě ő ș ț ế ệ), so Русский, Українська, Ελληνικά, Čeština and Tiếng Việt sit on the stamp sheet in one design. Leaving the other seven scripts to the system costs 0 bytes and shows each script in the face its own readers' phones already use. Budget: about 108 KB base, about 145 KB with every slice.

styles.navigation: The top flap is the microsite's whole nav: the wordmark (back to the top of the sheet) and five links (Modes, Editions, Postage, Privacy, Questions). Every fold line names the panel below it, so scrolling reads like unfolding. On mobile, 'Contents' opens a fold-down panel listing every panel of the sheet as links; Esc or a second tap closes it. Focus is a 3px sheet-ink outline offset 3px; stamps also get a red perforation ring.
styles.signatureInteraction: 'Affix a stamp.' The 33 stamps are <button aria-pressed> elements in a CSS-grid sheet. Activating one runs about 1 KB of vanilla JS that copies its data-endonym, data-code, data-domain and (once gathered) data-articles onto the address label in 'Addressed the way they read it', for example '日本語 · ja.wikipedia.org · JAPANESE'. The violet cancel re-strikes over the chosen stamp (scale 1.06→1, 160ms) and an aria-live line announces the change. German keeps its eight real category names; other editions show their domain and size, never made-up category names. No-JS fallback: the sheet is a static, fully readable list of 33 editions with codes and domains, and the label shows the documented German address. Reduced motion: the label text swaps with no strike.
styles.motionGrammar: Paper-physical and brief. A panel's dashed fold line draws once as it enters (stroke-dashoffset, 300ms). The cancel strikes once when the Today-in-History panel enters (scale 1.04→1, 160ms). The sticky label slides up in 220ms ease-out, and stamps lift 2px on hover. There is no parallax, no floating envelope, no loop and no count-up. With prefers-reduced-motion everything is static and the sticky strip simply appears.
styles.readModeVariant: Privacy, support and the two alternatives pages are single letters on the same sheet. Each keeps the top flap nav, the chevron edge (sides on desktop, top on mobile) and a short address strip as masthead; on /alternatives/kiwix/ the strip reads 'To: readers comparing Kiwix · WanderWiki vs Kiwix'. The reading column is a label-white letter panel set in Ysabeau 400 at 18px/1.65 with a 68ch measure, and quick_answer opens the letter at 21px. Comparison tables are set as tariff tables. 'Pick WanderWiki if… / Use Kiwix if…' become Deliver-to and Return-to-sender lists. The privacy policy runs under 'Secrecy of correspondence', with the transparency record's facts in a declaration-form box. Support is 'Write to us': the email as an address label, response_time, and what to include.

fixes.text: Re-derive every visitorPath from the world's own reading order, and enforce two rules. styles.label: Today's Leaf
styles.lineage: The tear-off day calendar: the Soviet отрывной календарь and the German Abreißkalender, whose leaf backs carried a short article, an anniversary or a recipe and continued long pieces 'on the next leaf'; the Finnish almanac's day rows; and the American Page-A-Day block. Its grammar: a thick block of thin leaves glued under a printed binding strip, on a coloured backing card with a punched hanging hole. Each leaf has a perforation row, a giant condensed date numeral over the month and weekday, Sundays and holidays printed red, and reading on the reverse.
styles.thesis: The page is the day's leaf of a tear-off block: the front is a date and what happened on it, from Wikipedia's On This Day feed; the back is a short piece of reading; and every section below is the next leaf. It is a finite block you tear through and put down, not a feed. It refuses the starry 'universe of knowledge' phone page and the infinite card feed.

type.rationale: Calendar leaves are printed in tall, heavy, condensed grotesques, so one day fills a leaf and a month fits a strip. styles.signatureInteraction: 'Tear to today.' The tab on the hero leaf's perforation is rendered by JS. On tap, about 2 KB of vanilla JS requests en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/feed/onthisday/selected/MM/DD for the visitor's local date. The request is made only on click, with no cookies and nothing sent to Lagerland, and the leaf shows 'fetching' while it waits. The current leaf then tears away (transform-origin at the binding, rotateX to −14deg, translateY −60px, opacity to 0, 450ms), revealing a new leaf with today's numeral and weekday (red on a Sunday) and three real entries. Each entry links to its article with 'From Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0'. No-JS: the verified 13 May leaf stays and the tab never renders. Offline or on error, the leaf stays and small print says it couldn't reach Wikipedia. Reduced motion: the new leaf replaces the old one with no tear.
styles.motionGrammar: One verb: tear. As a leaf scrolls out past the top, it lifts from its binding and falls away (CSS animation-timeline: view(); rotateX ≤ 12deg, translateY, opacity), and one leaf edge leaves the stack. 'Tear to today' is the same motion at 450ms. Numerals never count up, nothing loops and the card has no parallax. Without scroll-timeline support (Firefox) leaves simply scroll. With prefers-reduced-motion leaves are static panels with perforated tops.

styles.label: Thirty-Three Originals
styles.lineage: Facing-page dual-language editions: the Loeb Classical Library (since 1912; Greek volumes in green cloth, Latin in red, the original on the left page and English on the right, with running heads and folios), dtv zweisprachig and Penguin Parallel Text. Also the Complutensian Polyglot (Alcalá, 1514–17), which set Hebrew, Latin and Greek in parallel columns, each in its own fount. And the scholarly page's apparatus, which collates other witnesses by siglum at the foot. Grammar only: no publisher name, logo or cover design.
styles.thesis: The page is an open facing-page edition whose two pages are honestly not translations of each other. The left page always carries a Wikipedia edition's own words (its endonym, its category tree, its On This Day keys); the right carries WanderWiki's English reading. The form readers expect to be a translation proves the app's real claim: each of the 33 editions is its own encyclopedia, queried in its own words. It refuses the starry 'universe of knowledge' phone page and the white Wikipedia look-alike.
styles.scene: A commuter on a morning train with a dual-language paperback open on their knee, under flat, even carriage daylight → light.
styles.colorStrategy: Restrained. Cool white page stock and black ink carry nearly everything. One green, Loeb's Greek cloth, marks every original-language word plus the running heads, folios and links. The deeper case-cloth green appears only as the edge around the open book, the top band, the sticky band and the colophon.

Gentium's extended Latin, Greek, Cyrillic and Vietnamese glyphs for the endonyms are also subset once (about 10 KB) instead of loading the 58 KB latin-ext slice.
type.rationale: SIL drew Gentium 'for the nations': one design covering Latin with every diacritic, Greek and Cyrillic, made for multilingual scholarly text. That is what a polyglot demands, so the English copy and Čeština, Tiếng Việt, Ελληνικά and Русский share one hand. Its low-contrast, faintly calligraphic roman reads as a book face, neither a news serif nor a fashion Didone, and none of the training-default serifs. Scripts it does not cover are set in matched Noto Serif cuts, as the Complutensian gave each column its own fount. Budget: about 68 KB for Gentium 400, 700 and 400i, plus about 10 KB of extended glyphs and about 25 KB of script subsets, about 103 KB in all.

styles.navigation: The top cloth band is the nav: the WanderWiki wordmark and Contents · Editions · Prices · Questions. Contents opens the book's contents page, listing every spread by title and folio: a full-height overlay on mobile, a dropdown page on desktop. Running heads link back to Contents. The green ribbon tracks the current spread in the gutter (sticky within each spread), so the reader always sees where in the book they are. Focus is a 3px original-green outline offset 3px; on the cloth band it is page white.
styles.signatureInteraction: 'Read the frontispiece.' Each of the 33 endonyms is a real link to its row in the Editions table further down (this is the no-JS behaviour). With JS (about 1 KB), a tap instead opens the edition's read-out in place, in the verso's apparatus line (aria-live polite), e.g. 'Deutsch · de · de.wikipedia.org · about 3.0M articles (List of Wikipedias, 2026) · written by its own editors, not a translation of English'. A 'see all 33' link goes to the table. The tapped name is underlined in original green and the others dim to 70% opacity, never below AA. Reduced motion: no fade; the read-out text simply appears.
styles.motionGrammar: Book-still. Spreads do not animate in. The ribbon slides between spreads (200ms) as the reader scrolls, the frontispiece read-out fades in over 120ms, and the sticky cloth band slides up in 200ms. There is no page curl, no parallax on plates, and nothing counts up or loops. With prefers-reduced-motion the ribbon jumps and the fades go.
styles.readModeVariant: Privacy, support and the two alternatives pages are single pages of the same book: a recto only, no spread. Each has the cloth band and edge, a running head (e.g. 'COLLATION · WANDERWIKI · KIWIX') and a Gentium 19px/1.6 reading column at 66ch, with quick_answer as the 'Argument' paragraph. Comparison tables become collation tables with sigla heads over the full names. 'Pick WanderWiki if… / Use Kiwix if…' become two facing lists on desktop and sequential lists on mobile. styles.risk: This is the bookish world the calibration warns about (serif on book pages). It survives only as cool white and green in low-contrast Gentium, with no cream, no italic display and no tracked mono labels. A facing-page form implies translation, and WanderWiki explicitly does not translate, so every spread has to carry its 'not a translation' line or visitors will misread the product. On phones the spread collapses to single pages, losing the facing effect where most visitors are. The frontispiece needs a data pull and seven script subsets. It is the least instantly 'app-like' of the three, since screenshots appear only as plates from the fourth spread on. AppMeta's 'Fifty-Language Leaflet' is also multilingual; this stays a bound facing-page book (spreads, gutter, cloth, Gentium), never a folded leaflet with language tabs.
styles.memoryTest: The page that was an open book: the 33 Wikipedia language names on the left page, each sized by how big that Wikipedia is, facing 'Swipe. Learn. Repeat.'; and further in, 'Wissenschaft, Physik, Chemie' facing 'Science'.

fixes.text: Re-derive every visitorPath from the world's own reading order, and enforce two rules. (1) Within a surface, no two styles may share the relative order of more than two of {price, screenshots, comparison, privacy record, founder, FAQ}. (2) At least one style per surface must change GROUPING, not just order: for example, FAQ split into the sections it answers, who_for/who_not_for folded into the price, or the privacy record as the opener. World-native examples: tare-b sets Puzzle No. 1 before the Rules and puts price and answers at the back like a book. studio-a, allpaid-c and rightsplit-a open with the record (bin label, statement, label data) before any feature. soon-b prints the fare and stub (price) on the face, first. gymlogger-x-c shows the plateau formula before any offer. xiangqiful-c files each FAQ as a margin question on the entry it concerns. observa-b ends on 'past issues' (release notes) instead of a closing CTA block. The maker/freshness line and the shared footer strip may stay common.

Add one production task to every style: a one-off script in scripts/ (already excluded from the build, so it is not a deploy build step) that commits derivatives. Icons at 64, 128 and 256px (WebP plus a PNG fallback, about 15 KB or less at 128). Screenshots at 400w, 800w and 1200w WebP (about 40, 90 and 160 KB or less). The studio mark as the clean SVG that studio a/b/c already ask for. Front matter keeps the original paths; one include maps them to the derivatives and emits width/height, srcset/sizes, loading=lazy and decoding=async (eager plus fetchpriority=high only for a single hero image).

Make it a global contract: html { scroll-padding-top: var(--sticky-top); scroll-padding-bottom: var(--sticky-bottom) }, so focus and anchors never land under a bar. Allow one sticky element per edge, pad the bottom bar with env(safe-area-inset-bottom), and on viewports shorter than 600px hide the top strip while the bottom bar is showing.

Subset each script with pyftsubset --text='<endonym>' --layout-features='*' so the shaping closure is kept. Commit the outputs and the script in scripts/, and load each file with a unicode-range so only scripts present on the page are fetched. Budget: Gentium Book Plus 400/700/400i is 66 KB, plus 35 KB or less for the seven subsets.
